name: Colombia
summary_text: Colombia has one of Latin America's strongest legal frameworks — Constitutional Court legal gender recognition since 1993 (no surgery required, based on self-recognition), "trans" and "non-binary" ID markers (November 2025), a Comprehensive Trans Law being legislated (2025), marriage equality (2016), and a Constitutional Court ruling protecting a trans inmate from prison violence. President Petro's government is pro-LGBTIQ+. But the law-versus-practice gap is extreme and violent. More than 40 trans women were killed in a single year, with armed groups running "social cleansing" campaigns (Caquetá) and posting kill-lists targeting specific LGBTQ individuals ("All will be military targets"). Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was tortured and murdered in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, with a viral video of the assault. The UN Independent Expert urged Colombia to "close the gap between laws and lived realities amid rising violence." For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Bogotá's Chapinero district is a well-established LGBTQ+ area. The armed-group violence is concentrated in conflict regions and targets local communities, not tourists — but the organized targeting is a distinctive, severe concern.

sources.title: The transphobic murder that has shocked Colombia | International | EL PAÍS English
sources.claim_summary: El País (April 2025): the transphobic murder of Sara Millerey, 32, in Bello, Antioquia - thrown into a creek with fractured limbs and left to drown, filmed - shocked Colombia and terrified the trans community; her family demands justice.

sources.title: Sara Millerey’s brutal murder shocked Colombia. The killings didn’t stop there | CNN
sources.claim_summary: CNN (Aug 2025): 'Sara Millerey's brutal murder shocked Colombia. The killings didn't stop there' — investigation into continued attacks and killings of trans women and LGBT people with little accountability.

sources.title: ‘We are killed for what we are’: trans women in Colombia targeted by armed groups | Global development | The Guardian
sources.claim_summary: The Guardian (July 2024): more than 40 trans women were killed in Colombia the previous year; armed groups in Caquetá are threatening a wave of 'social cleansing' - trans women report being killed 'for what we are' and repeatedly forced to flee.

sources.title: Sobre el acceso a derechos económicos, sociales y culturales de personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia – Colombia Diversa
sources.claim_summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Colombia Diversa page addresses access to rights for LGBTIQ people in Colombia.

sources.title: Colombia | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): strong legal protections - 1999 Constitutional Court rulings restricting nonconsensual intersex surgeries; same-sex marriage since 2011 (refusals illegal since 2016); adoption since 2015; simplified legal gender recognition since 2015; third-gender classification for nonbinary people recognised March 2022; 2025 court order against a volleyball league regulator for discrimination.

sources.title: Colombia urged to close gap between LGBT rights laws and lived realities amid rising violence - JURIST - News
sources.claim_summary: JURIST (May 2025): UN Independent Expert Graeme Reid, concluding a fact-finding mission across Colombia, praised legal reforms but warned of a stark gap between institutional progress and lived reality - discrimination and violence persist, particularly against trans women and those facing intersecting marginalisation (migrants, Indigenous people, youth, persons with disabilities).

sources.title: Protegen derechos de mujer trans privada de la libertad que fue objeto de violencia y discriminación | Ámbito Jurídico
sources.claim_summary: Ambito Jurídico (in Spanish): Colombian court protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty - ruling on treatment of trans detainees.

EFE (Nov 2025, in Spanish): Colombia's Registraduría announced citizens will be able to mark 'trans' and 'no binario' in the sex field of identity documents - 'a key step' for recognising gender-diverse identification.

sources.title: Colombia Allows Transgender Community To Change Sex On IDs Without Physical Exams | IBTimes
sources.claim_summary: International Business Times (June 2015): Colombia allowed trans people to change name and sex on ID cards without physical or psychiatric examinations - a notarised declaration replaces the previous 'cumbersome' process that involved judges ordering bodily inspections; Justice Minister Yesid Reyes approved the decree.
